nameStory: This grass gets its "windmill" name from its distinctive flower clusters that radiate out like the spokes of a windmill. The "tumble" part comes from its habit of breaking off at the base when mature and rolling across the landscape like a tumbleweed, scattering seeds as it goes.
description: Tumble windmillgrass is a warm-season annual grass that forms small clumps about 1-3 feet tall. It has narrow, bluish-green leaves and produces distinctive flower clusters that look like tiny windmills at the tips of its stems. This southwestern native occasionally shows up in New England, likely arriving as a hitchhiker in soil or seed mixes.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: The unmistakable "windmill" flower clusters have 6-15 narrow spikes radiating from a single point like wheel spokes, each spike about 2-4 inches long and purplish when young

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat leaves about 1/8 to 1/4 inch wide with a distinctive bluish-green or grayish-green color that feels smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose tufts or small clumps rather than spreading runners, with multiple stems arising from the base in a bunch-like pattern

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds have fluffy white hairs that catch the wind, and the whole plant may break off and tumble when dry and mature

habitat: Look for this uncommon grass in disturbed, sandy or gravelly soils along roadsides, construction sites, or waste areas. It prefers full sun and well-drained conditions, often appearing where soil has been imported or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up. Young plants are small tufts of narrow, bluish-green leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly and produce their characteristic windmill-like flower clusters from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and plants turn tan or brown, often breaking off at the base to tumble and disperse seeds.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only scattered seeds to potentially germinate the following year.

funFact: This grass can literally go bowling for biology - when it breaks off and tumbles in the wind, a single plant can travel for miles, dropping up to 40,000 seeds along its journey like nature's own seed-spreading roadshow.
confusionNotes: The windmill-like flower arrangement is so distinctive that it's unlikely to be confused with any other New England grass. Other grasses may have finger-like flower clusters, but none radiate from a single point quite like this species.
contextualKnowledge: This is actually a southwestern U.S. native that's considered weedy in its home range. Its rare appearances in New England are likely temporary introductions rather than established populations, as our climate isn't ideal for long-term survival.
compareHints: As the only windmillgrass documented in New England, compare it to finger grasses like crabgrass, which have similar radiating flower spikes but typically fewer of them (3-7 vs 6-15) and they don't form as perfect a circular pattern. The bluish leaf color also sets it apart from most common New England grasses.
